football_evidence.question: Can Oklahoma keep Kentucky behind schedule?
football_evidence.assessment: No material disagreement: EdgeDesk and the line are within 1.8 points.
supporting: When Kentucky has the ball (pass protection against the pass rush): Kentucky’s offense has allowed a sack on 7.2% of its dropbacks, and Oklahoma’s defense sacks the quarterback on 11.4% of opponent dropbacks (FBS average 5.7%).
When Kentucky has the ball (third down): Kentucky’s offense converts 26.1% of its third downs, and Oklahoma’s defense allows opponents to convert 25.7% of their third downs (FBS average 39.5%).
In his last two games (South Alabama and South Carolina), Minchey averaged 6.8 yards per attempt, against 9.4 in his three games before that.
EdgeDesk’s position-group ratings put Oklahoma’s defensive line No. 5 nationally and Kentucky’s No. 74.
contradicting: When Oklahoma has the ball (big plays on the ground): Oklahoma’s offense turns 2.5% of its runs into explosive gains, and Kentucky’s defense gives up explosive gains on 4.9% of opponent runs (FBS average 6.6%).

When Kentucky has the ball (big plays on the ground): Kentucky’s offense turns 10.2% of its runs into explosive gains, and Oklahoma’s defense gives up explosive gains on 5.3% of opponent runs (FBS average 6.6%).

When Kentucky has the ball (the line of scrimmage on running plays): Kentucky’s offense is stopped at or behind the line on 13.8% of its runs, and Oklahoma’s defense stops 16.8% of opponent runs at or behind the line (FBS average 17.4%).
EdgeDesk’s position-group ratings put Kentucky’s running backs No. 16 nationally and Oklahoma’s No. 91.
quarterbacks: John Mateer has completed 72 of 110 passes (65.5%) for 903 yards, 8.2 yards per attempt, 8 touchdowns and 4 interceptions in four games for Oklahoma, and has been sacked on 7 of 117 dropbacks.
Kenny Minchey has completed 94 of 140 passes (67.1%) for 1,144 yards, 8.2 yards per attempt, 10 touchdowns and 1 interception in five games for Kentucky, and has been sacked on 11 of 151 dropbacks.

Oklahoma’s offense has to hold its own on long runs against a defense that gives up explosive gains on 4.9% of opponent runs.
Oklahoma’s defense has to slow Kentucky on long runs — Kentucky’s offense turns 10.2% of its runs into explosive gains.
Oklahoma’s defense has to come out ahead in the pass-rush matchup: it sacks the quarterback on 11.4% of opponent dropbacks, against an offense that has allowed a sack on 7.2% of its dropbacks.
